newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rescuers hear sounds in Australia landslide rubble.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers hear sounds in Australia landslide rubble.

text.p: Rescue workers who had almost despaired of finding anyone alive heard muffled sounds on Saturday under the rubble of two Australian ski lodges destroyed by a landslide, police said.
"We've head muffled sounds under the concrete slabs," police spokesman Mark Hargraves told reporters. "They (rescue workers) are going berserk up there trying to move as much rubble as they can".
Twenty people are thought to have been entombed in Wednesday night's landslide in the ski village of Thredbo, in Australia's Snowy Mountains, when a slope gave way, destroying two lodges.

"Our hopes are that it's a voice and that we're gpoing to get there as soon as possible," Hargraves said. "The rescuers have been extremely encouraged by this," he said, adding that the sounds "could take some time to reach".

Police earlier put the confirmed death toll at three, revising it downwards from four. The body of a man was recovered on Thursday. Two other bodies were sighted on Friday by rescue workers but have not recovered.
Search crews had worked in the mangled wreckage all through the night under lights in freezing conditions and reported hearing the sounds as dawn broke.
Hopes had been turning to despair of ever finding someone alive in the wreckage of the two lodges.
A massive weight of concrete slabs, stacked in a precarious heap where many of the missing were believed trapped, is being painstakingly sawn into pieces before being hoisted free.
Frustration had earlier begun to show on the faces of search crews whose efforts were being stalled by the instability of the slope and fears that the mass of debris could slide further.
Family and friends of the victims have kept a grim vigil on the search, watching from a facing hillside for signs of life.
The temperature plunged well below freezing during the night for the third night since the landslide.
Police on Friday had virtually ruled out the chance of finding a survivor, saying the likelihood was "infinitesimally small".
Optic fibre cameras and thermal imaging equipment have failed to show signs of life in the wreckage of the Carinya and Bimbadeen lodges.
The work of picking through the rubble has been fraught with danger and hazards such as leaking fuel from crushed cars. The rubble is 10 metres (35 feet) deep in places.
"I am quite confident they (family and friends) understand the enormity of the task that faces us," Superintendent Charlie Sanderson told reporters on Friday night.
Earlier on Friday, distraught Thredbo villagers touched by the landslide gathered at their small, sunlit church to pray for survivors and mourn those confirmed dead.
Messages of sympathy poured in from around the world to the small, close-knit community which swells to 4,000 in the skiing season from a summer population of about 500.

Britain's Queen Elizabeth, who is also Australia's head of state, sent a message of sympathy to the victims' friends and families, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer cut short an official visit to Japan, and Prime Minister John Howard issued a special statement of sympathy from his hospital bed.
Church services were held around the country.
Police have said those buried included a middle-aged couple from California, a New Zealand woman and 17 Australians.
Experts believe seepage from a mountain spring may have caused the earth to give way.
